analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated federal office to investigate and sue over unfair, monopolistic practices by meat and poultry packers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Agriculture Committee and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a new Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters inside the Agriculture Department's Packers and Stockyards Division. That office would investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act — the century-old law meant to stop meatpackers from using unfair, discriminatory, or monopolistic practices against farmers, ranchers, and consumers — with subpoena power and the ability to bring civil cases. It was introduced in February 2025, referred to the House Agriculture Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who often face higher meat prices when a few large packers dominate the market, and independent farmers and ranchers who sell livestock to those packers and can be squeezed on price and contract terms. The office would give them an enforcement body focused specifically on their industry's competition problems.

how_it_helps.text: The new office would use all available tools, including subpoenas, to investigate and prosecute unfair, deceptive, discriminatory, and monopolistic practices in livestock, meat, and poultry markets.
It would coordinate competition enforcement with the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission and coordinate food-supply security with the Department of Homeland Security.

It would give the Special Investigator direct authority to bring any civil or administrative action authorized under the Packers and Stockyards Act, rather than leaving every case to generalist agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Large meat and poultry packers, who would face a dedicated investigator with subpoena power able to sue them under the Packers and Stockyards Act. Taxpayers would fund the new office and its staff of attorneys.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large meatpackers, and taxpayers for the office

drawbacks.text: The bill's main mechanism is a new office with dedicated attorneys and subpoena power, which costs federal money and could overlap with enforcement work USDA, DOJ, and the FTC already do.

The Packers and Stockyards Act already gives USDA enforcement authority; the bill changes who enforces the law, not what conduct is illegal, so critics could argue it does not strengthen the underlying rules themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill creates a dedicated enforcement office to police a market where a few large packers buy from many independent ranchers; the main cost is a new federal office and spending, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that a new office only helps if it is funded and used aggressively — enforcement power on paper does not lower prices by itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Agriculture Committee, which never voted on it, so it died when the bill was left sitting in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Gottheimer introduced the Meat and Poultry Special Investigator Act on February 14, 2025, with two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat.
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee the same day; it was later sent to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry, where no further action was taken.

The bill would have created a Special Investigator for Competition Matters within USDA's Packers and Stockyards Division, with subpoena power and authority to sue over violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meat and poultry packers, who avoid a dedicated antitrust-style investigator focused on their industry; shoppers and independent ranchers gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large meatpackers; no investigator was created

for.name: House Committee on Agriculture
for.what_they_did: Received the bill at introduction and never advanced it to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor — but never reached the stage where party positions could be measured in a vote.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry packers and processors
industries.note: The bill creates a dedicated enforcement office to investigate and sue packers over monopolistic and unfair practices, so large processors face more litigation and investigation risk. Its power depends on how aggressively it is staffed and used.

industries.industry: Independent livestock producers, farmers, and ranchers
industries.note: The Packers and Stockyards Act exists to safeguard farmers and ranchers from unfair treatment by dominant packers; a dedicated investigator gives them a stronger enforcement channel. Farmers and consumers pay through taxes for the office, but the intended trade is fairer markets.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a House Agriculture subcommittee with only two cosponsors; in this Congress it is unlikely to be scheduled for a markup or floor vote unless leadership elevates it, and a similar proposal has previously stalled.
